senses.gloss:
pitā
(‘one who protects’)
------------------------------------------
The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (1.11) declares that the ड़थेर् is only next to the मोथेर् and should be honoured like a god. This is but proper since he gives birth, एदुचतिओन् and culture to his offspring.
According to the smṛtis it is the ड़थेर् who performs the उपनयन sacrament and imparts the sacred गायत्री-मन्त्र to his sons.
Whether the ड़थेर् has a sense of ownership over his sons has been a debatable point.
As regards the division of ancestral property, he could unequally distribute it among his sons in the ancient days though in later days it became mandatory to distribute it equally.
If he dies before clearing all his debts, his sons and grandsons were obliged to clear the same.
According some dharmaśāstra works the following are pitās or ‘fathers’: अन्न-dātā (one who gives ड़ोओद्); bhayatrātā (one who protects from dangers); śvaśura (father-in-law); janitā (father); upanetā (one who performs उपनयन).

pitṛpakṣa
(‘the fortnight dedicated to the forefathers’)
------------------------------------------
The 15 days of the dark fortnight of the month Bhādrapada, are called ‘Pitṛpakṣa’ or ‘Mahālayapakṣa’ and the new-मोओन् day as ‘Mahālaya अमावास्या’. These days are considered to be extremely auspicious for performing the obsequial rites to the departed ancestors.
The story goes that कर्ण, the great hero of the Mahābhārata, could not get any ड़ोओद् to eat when he went, after his death, to the higher regions, though he could get plenty of silver and gold there. This was because he had donated plenty of gold and silver but not ड़ोओद्! Distressed much, he prayed to यम, the god of death, and through his grace returned to this earth during this Mahālayapakṣa, gifted plenty of ड़ोओद् and then returned. Hence, annadāna or giving ड़ोओद् to the hungry, is an important duty enjoined in the observance of these days.
On all the fifteen days, offerings are made to the departed manes, including those whose names or manner of death are not known.
Men of the family generally observe some austerities during this period, like not shaving the hair or the beard, not paring the nails and so on. Feeding the priests with khīr or pāyasa (pudding) during this period is considered to be highly pleasing to the पितृस् or manes.

pitṛs
(‘fathers,’ ‘ancestors’)
------------------------------------------
The Sanskrit word ‘pitṛ’ becomes ‘pitā’ in the singular and ‘pitaraḥ’ in the plural. Whereas the former means ‘father’, the latter has been used in several senses such as forefathers or ancestors, a type of semi-divine beings inhabiting their own world called पितृलोक, certain types of sages and so on.
The most common meaning as used in śrāddhas (obsequial rites) is three generations of ancestors: ड़थेर्, grand-ड़थेर् and great-grandfather. It is believed that during the performance of śrāddhas these पितृस् accept the offerings in the form of birds or by entering into the invitee ब्राह्मणस् through their subtle bodies.
According to another version (Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa ch. 45) they were created as a separate class of beings along with देवस् (gods), राक्षसस् (demons) and mānavas (human beings), by ब्रह्मा the creator himself.
They are also, sometimes, identified with the Saptaṛṣis or the seven sages, the progenitors of mankind, as the originators of gotras or lineages.
Several classes of पितृस् such as Aṅgirasas, Vairūpas or Bhṛgus have been mentioned in the Ṛgvedic verses (vide 10.14.5 and 6). Occasionally they have also been divided into three grades by the same Veda (10.15.1).
The पितृस् can be satiated through proper rites and they can bless their descendants by granting boons.
See also ŚRĀDDHA.

Pitṛyāna
(‘the path of manes’)
------------------------------------------
Literally, the word means the path by which a pitṛ or a dead ancestor goes to the Candraloka or the world of the मोओन्.
We find from the उपनिषद्स् (and even the Bhagavadgītā 8.24-26) that the ancient Hindus believed in two paths by which the सोउल् of a dead person could go, either to the ब्रह्मलोक or to the Candraloka.
The former was called देवयान (or Arcirādimārga) and the latter as पितृयान (or Dhūmādimārga).
The various stations mentioned in the पितृयान are: dhūma (smoke), रात्रि (night), aparapakṣa (dark fortnight), दक्षिणायन (southern solstice), पितृलोक (world of manes), आकाश (space), and Candramas ([world of] Somarāja or the king मोओन्).
These words represent the various guides on the path.
Those who perform Vedic rites like अग्निहोत्र and public utility activities like digging wells or planting trees etc., go by this path to the Candraloka (the world of the मोओन्) and return to the earth after exhausting their religious merit. This world (Candraloka) is more like a हेअवेन् from which there is return.
See DEVAYĀNA for more details.

pitṛyajña
(‘sacrifice unto the forefathers’)
------------------------------------------
See PAÑCAMAHĀYAJÑAS.

pitṛmedha
(‘forefather-sacrifice’)
------------------------------------------
The word actually means consigning the dead-body of a forefather to the fire of च्रेमतिओन् which is similar to a medha or a sacrifice.
This ancient custom comprised four stages: च्रेमतिओन्, collecting the charred bones and depositing them underground in an urn, expiatory rites and erection of a monument (generally a pole or a staff).
Depositing the urn at the root of a tree or casting the contents in the गङ्गा river were also practised.
If the deceased person was an आचार्य (spiritual or Vedic preceptor) or a श्रोत्रिय (learned in the वेदस्) the rite was called brahmamedha. The special mantras known as caturhotā (vide Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.3.11.4; 1.3.1.1; 3.12.5.1; 2.2.3.5; 2.3.1.3; 2.3.1.1; and 2.2.8.2) were chanted on this occasion.

Pitṛgāthā
(‘song of the manes’)
------------------------------------------
In हिन्दुइस्म्, the पितृस् (forefathers or manes) have always been respected. Normally, once a year, the descendants are expected to pay homage to them through religious rites known as Śrāddhas.
It seems that—even as the descendants are eager to appease their pitṛs—the पितृस् too hanker for such appeasement.
The Matsyapurāṇa (204.3-17), one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, contains an interesting piece, depicting such hankering. This has come to be known as the Pitṛgāthā or the Song of the Manes. It is to be chanted as a part of śrāddha ceremonies, thus making the ब्राह्मणस् invited for ड़ोओद्, listen to it.
The gāthā expresses the desire of the पितृस् to get good ड़ोओद् (in the śrāddhas), receive oblations of water in holy rivers, and get a śrāddha performed at the holy pilgrim centre गया (in Bihar). They will bless their descendants who donate a milch-cow and a deerskin to a good ब्राह्मण, who will set free a bull to roam about as it likes, who will donate gold or cow or a piece of land to a deserving and needy person, who will perform public service activities such as digging a well for drinking water and raising a nice garden.
However, they are pleased immensely if their descendants become scholars in the scriptures and great devotees of Lord विष्णु.

pitṛ-ṛṇa
(‘debt to the manes’)
------------------------------------------
Every human being—according to Hinduism—is said to be born under three ṛṇas or debts. Among these, the पितृ-ऋण is the second. This ṛṇa or debt can be repaid by marrying according to धर्म and having a son who will perform śrāddhas to the पितृस् or departed ancestors thereby appeasing them.
See ṚṆATRAYA for details.

pitṛloka
(‘the world of [dead] ancestors’)
------------------------------------------
Just as a human being does not want to be destroyed after the death of his body, he also does not want his forefathers and ancestors to be destroyed after their death. The belief that one’s dead-ancestors live in a separate world is common to most of the peoples of the world.
The Ṛgveda (10.14.2 and 7) mentions the पितृलोक where one’s departed ancestors live.
The उपनिषद्स् consider the पितृलोक as a place that can be attained by one after death, by performing sacrifices like अग्निहोत्र (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.5.16), and also as a station on the path of पितृयान (the path of manes, the path of smoke) (ibid 6.2.16).
